meta.case_name: Rental Cars and Frequent Flyer Miles (BCG)

prompt.context: Our client is a US airline with a popular frequent flyer mile program. They sell frequent flyer miles through partnerships with credit card companies, hotels, and rental car agencies. While the business overall has been healthy, they have noticed a sharp decline in their frequent flyer miles revenue from the rental car segment: a 50% drop in the last two years. They have asked us to determine the cause for this loss in revenue, and what they can do to reverse the trend.
prompt.question: What is causing the 50% decline in frequent flyer miles revenue from the rental car segment over the last two years, and what can the client do to reverse this trend?

clarifying_info.q: How long has the frequent flyer program been in place?
clarifying_info.a: Over 20 years. It was created for competitive advantage and customer retention. This airline was among the first to have the program, but now almost every airline has frequent flyer miles.

clarifying_info.q: How do car rental agencies sell these miles?
clarifying_info.a: An agency advertises that customers can get X frequent flier miles per car rental day. When customers request the miles, they get them and the agency pays the airline for the transaction.

clarifying_info.q: How many rental car agencies are there and how many are partners?
clarifying_info.a: There are 7 major car rental agencies in the country. 5 out of 7 are partners with our client. These 5 agencies comprise 97% of all rental car business in the US.

clarifying_info.q: Has the volume of car rentals changed?
clarifying_info.a: No — number of cars rented has not gone down and days per rental have not gone down.

clarifying_info.q: Do frequent flyer members prefer rental cars that come with miles?
clarifying_info.a: Yes — it is fair to assume that frequent flyer members would strongly prefer to rent a car that came with miles as compared to one that did not.

exhibits.title: Math Assumptions for Exclusive Partnership Analysis
exhibits.shows: A set of quantitative assumptions provided to the candidate for sizing the rental agency partnership opportunity
exhibits.data: 10 MM rentals per year; $45 car rental per day on average; average rental is 3 days; approx 10% margins on car rentals for rental car agencies before paying for any frequent flier miles; 10M rentals/year by frequent flier members; assume 5 partners now, cut down to 3 partners; current payments from rental cars to client are $3 per transaction

framework: Diagnose revenue decline: revenue = price per mile x miles sold per transaction x number of transactions — identify which driver changed
Assess partnership structure: number of partners, volume allocation per partner, incentive alignment
Identify root cause: rental agencies wanted lower cost per transaction, asked airline to cut price per mile, airline refused, agencies responded by offering fewer miles per rental day
Explore solutions to reverse the trend: renegotiate pricing, exclusive partnerships, mandate minimum miles, auction partnerships
Quantify value of exclusive/semi-exclusive partnership to determine willingness to pay and potential revenue uplift
Consider implementation risks and other strategic extensions (hotels, partner selection criteria)

questions.prompt: What is the root cause of the revenue decline from rental car agencies?
questions.guidance: The number of rentals has not dropped. What decreased is the number of frequent flyer miles sold per rental day. The rental car companies wanted to lower their own costs per transaction by paying less for frequent flyer miles. They asked the airline to lower the price per mile; the airline refused. In response, the agencies simply started offering fewer miles per rental, reducing total miles sold and therefore revenue to the airline.

questions.prompt: Brainstorm possible solutions for the airline to reverse the revenue decline from rental car agencies.

Structure and solve the math: how much could the client benefit from moving to an exclusive (3-partner) arrangement? What is each rental agency's willingness to pay under the new model versus the current model?
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize fixed vs. variable costs matter — marginal profit from extra rentals should use variable costs only. For simplicity all fleet costs are assumed variable. Walk through: (A) current profit per agency, (B) potential profit per agency under 3-partner model, (C) total WTP comparison and revenue uplift to airline.

math.setup: Given: 10MM total ff-member rentals/year; $45/day; 3 days/rental; 10% margin before ff payment; $3 current ff payment per transaction; currently 5 partners, moving to 3 partners.
steps: A. Current profit to one rental agency from ff customers: Rentals per agency = 10MM / 5 = 2MM. Revenue per rental = $45 x 3 = $135. Gross profit before ff fee = 10% x $135 = $13.50. Net profit after ff fee = $13.50 - $3.00 = $10.50 per rental. Total profit per agency = $10.50 x 2MM = $21MM. Equivalently: gross profit = $13.50 x 2MM = $27MM; total ff fees paid = $3 x 2MM = $6MM; net = $21MM.

B. Potential profit to one agency under 3-partner model (same total rentals): Rentals per agency = 10MM / 3 = 3.33MM. Gross profit before ff fee = 10% x $135 x 3.33MM = $45MM. WTP for exclusive arrangement (per agency) = $45MM (total profit at stake). Incremental WTP vs. current arrangement = $45MM - $21MM = $24MM. Incremental vs. current fee paid = $24MM - $6MM = $18MM.
C. Total WTP comparison: WTP(new) = $24MM x 3 agencies = $72MM. WTP(old) = $6MM x 5 agencies = $30MM (assumes current fee = max WTP). Incremental revenue potential = $72MM - $30MM = $42MM.
math.answer: The exclusive 3-partner model could generate up to $42MM in additional annual revenue for the airline. Even capturing half (~$21MM) represents a ~67% increase in frequent flyer revenue from rental car agencies.

brainstorming.prompt: What options does the airline have to reverse the decline in frequent flyer revenue from rental car agencies?

categories.name: Partnership structure changes
ideas: Move to exclusive or semi-exclusive partnerships (fewer partners, higher per-partner value)
Auction partnership slots to determine maximum willingness to pay
Mandate a minimum number of ff miles offered per rental day as a contract term
Negotiate a higher price per mile tied to exclusivity premium

categories.name: Partner selection criteria
ideas: Select partners based on geographical coverage to maximize reach for ff customers
Survey ff customers on rental agency preference or use existing market share data among ff customers
Evaluate agencies by current transaction volume with ff members

categories.name: Risk and demand considerations
ideas: Assess whether customers have loyalty to particular agencies such that total rentals might shrink under exclusivity
Model fixed vs. variable cost split more precisely to better estimate agency profit impact
Evaluate whether customer switching costs are high enough to sustain volume under a limited-partner model

categories.name: Pricing and contract design
ideas: Price new partnership on a higher price-per-mile basis rather than mandating miles-per-day
Use tiered pricing based on exclusivity level (exclusive vs. preferred partner)
Benchmark against hotel partnership pricing model for consistency

categories.name: Strategic extensions
ideas: Explore similar exclusive or preferred partnership models with hotels
Evaluate whether the same dynamic (too many partners diluting value) affects hotel or credit card segments
Consider bundled partnership offers (rental + hotel exclusivity) for greater negotiating leverage

recommendation: The airline should move from a 5-partner model to a semi-exclusive 3-partner model for rental car agencies, capturing up to $42MM in incremental annual revenue from increased willingness to pay by the fewer, more privileged partners.
Even capturing 50% of this upside (~$21MM) represents a roughly 67% increase in frequent flyer revenue from the rental car segment, fully reversing and exceeding the decline.
risks: Customers may have loyalty to specific rental agencies not selected as partners, potentially reducing total rental volume and partially offsetting gains.
Excluded agencies may respond competitively, e.g., partnering with rival airlines, reducing the overall value of the client's ff program.
Actual fixed vs. variable cost split for agencies may differ from assumptions; if fixed costs are significant, the variable-cost-only profit estimate may overstate agency WTP.
next_steps: Survey frequent flyer members on rental agency preferences to guide partner selection.
Run an auction or structured negotiation process with the 5 current partners to reveal true WTP for exclusive slots.
Model fixed vs. variable cost breakdown for rental agencies to refine profit and WTP estimates.
Explore whether a similar exclusive partnership model could be applied to the hotel segment.
Define contract terms specifying minimum ff miles offered per rental day to prevent recurrence of the miles-reduction tactic.
